brief.head: Thinkers set the limit
brief.text: A coun­try can be much worse than its thinkers but never bet­ter, Ajay Shah said: they set its pro­duc­tion pos­si­bil­ity fron­tier, as Havel and Walesa did. {108-C06}

brief.head: Words that hide
brief.text: Havel told his ac­tors that lan­guage shapes re­al­ity. Amit Varma, quot­ing Jackson Katz, added that the pas­sive voice in “vi­o­lence against women” leaves out who is doing it. {108-C03}

brief.head: Write to think
brief.text: Gandhi and Ambedkar left dozens of vol­umes, Nehru long let­ters to chief min­is­ters. They were great thinkers partly be­cause they were pro­lific writ­ers, Amit Varma said. {108-C10}

brief.head: The strongman’s mask
brief.text: Nehru stayed a happy man through nine years of jail, jok­ing about him­self. The swag­ger of today’s strong­men, Ajay Shah said, masks inner weak­ness. {108-C09}

brief.head: Directors as funnels
brief.text: Every gov­ern­ment body, Ajay Shah ar­gued, needs a ma­jor­ity of in­de­pen­dent di­rec­tors: pri­vate peo­ple, not re­tired civil ser­vants, each a fun­nel for blunt out­side voices. {108-C15}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on five unlikely leaders
lead.head: Accidents will happen

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 108

body: Amit Varma opened with a test. If his friend were handed ab­so­lute power, would he take it for the good he could do, or turn it down? Ajay Shah did not hes­i­tate: “Get a bet­ter con­sti­tu­tion of India. What bet­ter use of ab­so­lute power?” {108-J01}

The episode was about peo­ple who never set out to hold power. The hosts had been talk­ing about Mark Carney, gov­er­nor of the Bank of England turned prime min­is­ter of Canada, and won­dered how many such ac­ci­den­tal politi­cians they could name.
They chose five: Carney, the Czech play­wright Václav Havel, Jawaharlal Nehru, Manmohan Singh and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
## Five ac­ci­dents

Carney, Shah said, was lifted by a col­lapse in Trudeau’s pop­u­lar­ity and by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Canada, which sent vot­ers to any plau­si­ble can­di­date who was not a right-wing con­ser­va­tive. Trump was “the crit­i­cal di­vine in­ter­ven­tion that got Mark Carney to power”. {108-S01}
Havel, barred from uni­ver­sity as a class enemy, be­came a dis­si­dent, spent years in prison and then be­came a pres­i­dent who re­fused to wear a tie.
Nehru, Shah ar­gued, was car­ried by a chain of ac­ci­dents, from two world wars to Gandhi’s choice. “It takes a Gandhi to choose a Nehru,” he said. {108-S10}
Manmohan Singh, un­like Carney, was ap­pointed at every step: Sonia Gandhi and Narasimha Rao, Shah said, had the good sense to pick him.
Zelenskyy, a co­me­dian who had played a pres­i­dent on tele­vi­sion, be­came one. When Russia in­vaded and, it is be­lieved, as­sas­sins came for him, he re­fused to flee. {108-S17}
## The case for out­siders
Varma then set out four pros and three cons. The first pro is that out­siders are gen­er­al­ists. A ca­reer politi­cian in India, he said, may never have had a pay­ing job.
The sec­ond is skin in the game of the real world. Leaders cut off from daily life, he ar­gued, pro­duce blun­ders like de­mon­eti­sa­tion.
The third is that the stakes are lower. Out of power, Varma said, Carney would go back to being a con­sul­tant. Shah widened the point: a good so­ci­ety is one where elec­tions are low stakes.

The fourth is that an out­sider has not spent decades in the re­peated game of money and power. “To sur­vive in pol­i­tics you need money, money will de­mand ROI,” Varma said. “It is straight away cor­rup­tion.” {108-C17}
## And the case against
Outsiders know the sys­tem less well. In 1991, Varma ar­gued, Manmohan Singh was right as fi­nance min­is­ter, but it took Narasimha Rao, an in­sider for decades, to do the pol­i­tics.
Shah re­called a Labour in­sider in Britain whose party re­turned to of­fice after a long time out: “we pressed the levers of power and noth­ing hap­pened.”
Outsiders may also know less pol­icy, and want bolder gam­bles than a party whose ca­reer politi­cians face elec­tion after elec­tion.

Will Zelenskyy win an elec­tion in peace­time? Shah re­minded lis­ten­ers that Churchill won the war and was booted out. Varma, who sees pol­i­tics as three sep­a­rate games of votes, party and gov­er­nance, an­swered: “we sim­ply don’t know.”
Shah tied the case for out­siders to in­tegrity. “It is not easy to turn around after a life­time of hav­ing forged a char­ac­ter to be­come a sim­ple deal maker,” he said.

second.label: Havel in power
second.head: Hungry for free speech
second.deck: Told whose view he had just rejected, Václav Havel did not back down

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Havel and the hungry man’s free speech

body: Václav Havel was due to meet Lee Kuan Yew, then Singapore’s leader, later that day. At a press con­fer­ence, the hosts’ friend Salil Tripathi asked him about the view that free speech mat­ters less than feed­ing a hun­gry per­son. {108-S06}

Havel dis­agreed at once. Then, as an af­ter­thought, he asked who held that view. “The per­son you’re meet­ing this af­ter­noon, sir,” Tripathi replied. You could hear a pin drop. Havel said he would make sure to tell Lee that he was wrong.

Meetings be­tween heads of state are usu­ally chore­ographed, said Amit Varma, who heard the story on *The Seen and the Unseen*. Havel stayed true to him­self. Varma voiced Havel’s tie re­fusal in Hindi, a lan­guage Havel did not know. {108-J06}

quote.text: If you do not have free speech, how will a hun­gry per­son be able to say that they are hun­gry?

third.head: Out of touch, out of notes

pic.caption: Amit Varma on demonetisation and the paan shop

body: Amit Varma wrote a se­ries of pieces against de­mon­eti­sa­tion. One, in the Times of India, went viral: Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal tweeted it. {108-S19}

He took apart each of Narendra Modi’s rea­sons. The key one, he said, was that Modi had not been a player in the real world for decades: “This man has not bought some­thing from a paan shop in fif­teen years.”

In 1978, when Indira Gandhi de­mon­e­tised, a thou­sand-rupee note was worth twelve thou­sand ru­pees in 2016 terms, he said. The 500-rupee note scrapped in 2016 was used every day, and the cash-based in­for­mal econ­omy was dev­as­tated.

Ajay Shah re­called George H. W. Bush, as­ton­ished on cam­era by a su­per­mar­ket bar­code scan­ner: “This is a guy who for twenty five years had never stepped out to buy any­thing for him­self.” {108-S20}

box.title: Havel, on the shelf
box.text: Amit Varma urged lis­ten­ers to read all of Havel’s plays, avail­able in English, and his ex­tended essay *The Power of the Powerless*, whose lat­est edi­tion car­ries an in­tro­duc­tion by Timothy Snyder. His mem­oir *To the Castle and Back* is “also a won­der­ful book”. {108-R05}

sections.label: The first accident
sections.head: Trump’s gift to Mark Carney
sections.caption: Mark Carney’s improbable rise
body: Mark Carney was a nor­mal pro­fes­sional cen­tral bank­ing type, Ajay Shah said, well re­spected and well trusted. In 2012, after scan­dals in the UK, the British ap­point­ment process chose this Canadian to run the Bank of England.

It worked, Shah ar­gued, be­cause in­fla­tion tar­get­ing in Canada is so much like in­fla­tion tar­get­ing in the UK, with ma­ture sta­tis­tics, good mod­els and strong re­search teams. “So ac­tu­ally then the knowl­edge be­comes por­ta­ble,” he said. {108-C01}

Back in Canada, Carney en­tered party pol­i­tics. Trudeau’s pop­u­lar­ity col­lapsed, and Trump’s threats in­flamed vot­ers. Unlike Manmohan Singh, ap­pointed at every step, Carney won fair and square, which gives him a dif­fer­ent level of au­thor­ity. Whether he can win again when Trump mat­ters less is, Shah said, an open ques­tion. {108-S01}
## Parties with­out own­ers

In the West, Amit Varma said, a suc­cess­ful banker can imag­ine a ca­reer in pol­i­tics; he named Mitt Romney. In India, “no re­spectable per­son is ac­tu­ally going to think of get­ting into pol­i­tics.”
Shah said India had paid too lit­tle at­ten­tion to the party as an in­sti­tu­tion. Parties, like firms, need rules, norms, cul­ture and a deep pool of tal­ent. {108-C02}

~ Varma said Nehru’s Congress had been like that. When a Ram idol was placed in the Babri Masjid, the UP chief min­is­ter Govind Ballabh Pant re­fused Nehru’s re­quest to re­move it. Indira Gandhi, he ar­gued, later hol­lowed the party out. {108-S02}

quote.text: Donald Trump is the crit­i­cal di­vine in­ter­ven­tion that got Mark Carney to power.

sections.label: The second accident
sections.head: Questions he could not answer
sections.caption: the playwright who became president
body: The com­mu­nists branded Václav Havel’s well-to-do fam­ily class en­e­mies, Amit Varma said, so Havel could not study phi­los­o­phy at uni­ver­sity. He took a job there as a lab tech­ni­cian in­stead, ar­riv­ing with his pock­ets stuffed with Kafka, Camus, Heidegger and Nietzsche.

A friend once saw him close a note­book he had been fill­ing fu­ri­ously. Its title, as Varma re­mem­bered it: “Questions I Cannot Answer”. In it Varma saw deep cu­rios­ity and deep hu­mil­ity. {108-S03}
His plays, such as *The Garden Party*, mock an empty bu­reau­cratic lan­guage that strips peo­ple of char­ac­ter. Havel told his ac­tors that lan­guage shapes re­al­ity.
## Prison, then pres­i­dency

After the Prague Spring of 1968 he be­came an out­spo­ken dis­si­dent, and he spent four con­tin­u­ous years in prison, from 1979 to 1983. {#prison} His let­ters to his wife were col­lected as *Letters to Olga*. {108-R03}

After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 he be­came pres­i­dent, but would not move into the palace or wear a tie. Asked why he was dressed like that, he said: “Because I rep­re­sent the peo­ple. The peo­ple are like this.” {108-S05}
~ Instead of sum­mits, Varma said, Havel in­vited Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones to per­form. {108-J05}

quote.text: If I am to be pun­ished, let it be for who I am.
quote.who: Václav Havel, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The third accident
sections.head: Crusader, not careerist
sections.caption: Nehru, the accidental prime minister
body: Jawaharlal Nehru won every elec­tion, Amit Varma said, but that is not how or why he started. The free­dom gen­er­a­tion were cru­saders for prin­ci­ples, not ca­reer politi­cians. Today, he said, pol­i­tics is “rival mafias fight­ing to get that mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence”.

Ajay Shah added a se­lec­tion ef­fect. Taking on the British Empire was so costly that only the best jumped: “when you have to jump, a very high ac­ti­va­tion en­ergy, only the best peo­ple will jump.” {108-C07}
## A writer in jail

Nehru spent nine years in British jails, Shah said, with­out heat­ing or air con­di­tion­ing but with books and note­books, and with­out beat­ings. “It was pretty,” Shah began. “Luxurious jail,” Varma fin­ished. {108-J10}

There Nehru wrote *Glimpses of World History* as let­ters to his daugh­ter, which Shah read as a child, and *The Discovery of India*, which he counts among the most im­por­tant the­o­ret­i­cal books about India. {108-R14}

Shah also cred­ited Nehru’s era with firmly sep­a­rat­ing civil­ian rule from the mil­i­tary. Liberation move­ments that took up guns, he said, tend to fall into cy­cles of vi­o­lence. “The means mat­ter.” {108-C08}
~ Gandhi chose Nehru over Rajaji mainly be­cause Nehru was much younger, Varma noted. “So it’s ironic that Rajaji ac­tu­ally out­lived Nehru.” {108-J09}

quote.text: Here you have a man lit­er­ally fif­teen min­utes be­fore the speech, scrib­bling on some ran­dom piece of tis­sue paper, and look at the writ­ing.

sections.label: The fourth accident
sections.head: When India was a dinky country
sections.caption: Manmohan Singh and 1991
body: Manmohan Singh began as an icon­o­clast, Ajay Shah said. In the 1960s Indian econ­o­mists agreed that India could not ex­port; in his PhD the­sis Singh was one of the first to dis­agree. Exporting, he ar­gued, is shaped by in­cen­tives: prices, cus­toms du­ties, ex­change rates. {108-S11}

Later, stranded in Geneva to head the South-South Commission after Ronald Reagan cut off UN fund­ing, Singh was res­cued by Percy Mistry, who lent the com­mis­sion a mil­lion pounds by per­sonal cheque. {108-S12}
## Legwork in Washington

By the late-1980s bal­ance of pay­ments cri­sis, Shah said, im­ports had stalled and fac­to­ries were clos­ing. “At that time India was a dinky coun­try,” he said. “Like ac­tu­ally no­body gave a damn about India.” {108-S13}
Singh trekked qui­etly be­tween the India ED’s of­fice, the US Treasury and the IMF. The gains of 1991 to 1993, Shah said, launched India into a dif­fer­ent orbit.

He com­pared Singh with Vajpayee: de­cency, coali­tions, good teams. Between them came 1991 to 2011, which Shah called “the most suc­cess­ful pe­riod in five thou­sand years of Indian his­tory”. {#fivethousand}

~ Amit Varma ad­mired his nerve too. In UPA-1, with the Left threat­en­ing to pull sup­port over the nu­clear deal, Singh said, as Varma told it: “This is one thing I’m putting my foot down on.” {108-S15}

quote.text: Success in ex­port­ing is shaped by in­cen­tives. It’s about prices, it’s about cus­toms du­ties, it’s about ex­change rates.

sections.label: The fifth accident
sections.head: Putin misreads the comedian
sections.caption: Putin’s three misreadings
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s, Ajay Shah said, is the most un­likely story in the world: a suc­cess­ful co­me­dian who had played a pres­i­dent in a tele­vi­sion se­ries.

Since 1991, when 94 per cent of Ukrainians voted to be their own coun­try, Russia had kept med­dling, back­ing a pro-Russian party, with guns too. “The game of mod­ern hy­brid war­fare is to pit a coun­try against it­self,” Shah said. {108-C11}

Ukraine also lacked ma­chin­ery. Poland, he said, took in twenty thou­sand pages of EU doc­u­ments on how to be a European coun­try. {#pages} Ukraine in­her­ited only the ar­bi­trary vi­o­lence of the USSR.
## Three mis­read­ings

Vladimir Putin, “deeply grounded in male­ness”, un­der­es­ti­mated three things, Shah ar­gued. He saw Zelenskyy as just a TV co­me­dian. He looked at Western Europe’s women de­fence min­is­ters and thought, “they’re women. What will they do?” And he took America’s chaotic exit from Afghanistan as weak­ness. {108-S16}
Amit Varma pointed out that the with­drawal was botched under Biden. The dates, Shah replied, were cho­sen by Trump.

~ Varma added a cre­den­tial Churchill, Nehru and Havel can­not match: “Zelenskyy played the piano with his dick.” Making a fool of your­self on stage night after night, he said, also takes courage. {108-J14}

quote.text: Putin thought this guy’s just a TV co­me­dian. What will he do?

sections.label: Pros and cons
sections.head: Four pros, three cons
sections.caption: the pros and cons of outsiders
body: Amit Varma set out four pros and three cons. The first pro: out­siders are gen­er­al­ists. Someone who leaves a suc­cess­ful ca­reer for pol­i­tics, he ar­gued, tends to have wider in­ter­ests than peers happy in their lane. {108-C13}
Politics it­self, he said, is three games: win­ning votes, ris­ing within party and leg­is­la­ture, and gov­ern­ing. Skill at one pre­dicts lit­tle about the oth­ers. {108-C12}
## Who tells the leader
The sec­ond pro is skin in the game. Varma would wel­come even a chai­wala, “as long as you’re an ac­tual chai­wala sell­ing chai at a train sta­tion.”

Ajay Shah added that knowl­edge reaches lead­ers through con­ver­sa­tion. A Havel or a Zelenskyy ar­rives with friends who “are not rev­er­en­tial be­cause you’ve just be­come a head of state.” {108-C14}

On the money that elec­tions de­mand, Varma re­cited a lim­er­ick from his days writ­ing them for the Times of India: “A neta who loves cur­rency notes / told me what his line of work de­notes. / It is kind of funny, we steal people’s money / and use some of it to buy their votes.” {108-J18}

~ Among the cons, out­siders know the sys­tem less well. Varma’s clas­sic ex­am­ple was the 1991 part­ner­ship: “Narasimha Rao could do the pol­i­tics and Manmohan could do the eco­nom­ics.” {108-C18}

quote.text: A politi­cian who comes to gov­ern­ment is not play­ing one game, they are play­ing three dif­fer­ent games.
So a good so­ci­ety is one where elec­tions are low stakes. So Kelkar al­ways says that in a good so­ci­ety, politi­cians should go out of of­fice, but never out of power.

p3.title: Tales of the unlikely
p3.deck: Four moments when accidental politicians showed what they were made of

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the night Russia came for Zelenskyy
stories.head: The comedian who would not leave
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy started out in show­biz, a very suc­cess­ful co­me­dian who played a pres­i­dent in a tele­vi­sion se­ries. Then he be­came one. Seen as a clean fig­ure out­side the usual mess, with a cam­paign heavy on so­cial media and the in­ter­net, he won 73 per cent of the vote. {#vote}
He was a lit­tle clue­less, Ajay Shah said, and made many mis­takes in the early days.

When Russia in­vaded in February 2022, Shah, like ev­ery­one else, ex­pected his gov­ern­ment to melt away, as Afghanistan’s had be­fore the Taliban. An ar­moured thrust from Belarus was aimed at Kyiv. Shah thought Zelenskyy would run to Lviv, or lead a gov­ern­ment in exile from Poland.
It is be­lieved that on the first night three sep­a­rate as­sas­si­na­tion teams came for his house. {#teams} He had a wife and two small chil­dren with him.
He woke up the next morn­ing and said he was not leav­ing. Offered a way out, he said: “My place is here, I need am­mu­ni­tion, not a ride.” {108-S17}
Amit Varma tried a punchier ver­sion: “I want ammo.” Shah held firm. “The exact line is my place is here, I need am­mu­ni­tion, not a ride.”

~ One by one, Western coun­tries saw that Ukraine would stand. “Would you re­ally send a lot of mil­i­tary kit to some­body who is about to fold?” Shah asked. He thinks Zelenskyy made the right calls every step of the way.
stories.why: Allies com­mit only when a leader has the stom­ach for a fight. Roosevelt once sent a trusted ad­viser, dying of can­cer, to Moscow to judge whether Stalin would stand and fight. The reply was short: yes. {108-S18}
stories.postscript: Zelenskyy ral­lied his peo­ple, Shah said, much as Churchill “picked up the words of the English lan­guage and hurled them into bat­tle”. {108-J15}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Zelenskyy’s choice to stay

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Charter 77 and a hesitant signatory
stories.head: The side she had already taken
body: In 1977 Václav Havel co-wrote Charter 77. He wanted a lot of peo­ple to sign it, Amit Varma said, so that it would seem the peo­ple of Czechoslovakia all be­lieved in it.
He went to one woman, a fel­low trav­eller. She agreed with him, she said, but sign­ing would be dan­ger­ous, and she was not sure she should take a side.
“You have al­ready taken a side,” Havel told her, “just not the one that you think you have.” She signed. {108-S04}

~ Varma heard in it the line at­trib­uted to Edmund Burke: evil tri­umphs when good men stand by and do noth­ing. Havel came back to the idea in 2008, cam­paign­ing for the Chinese dis­si­dent Liu Xiaobo to get the Nobel Prize: the crimes of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury, he said, began when good men stayed silent. {108-C04}

quote.text: Staying silent is also tak­ing a side.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the signatory who hesitated

stories.head: Et tu, Jawaharlal?
body: While Jawaharlal Nehru was prime min­is­ter, Ajay Shah said, a let­ter in the Hindustan Times warned that he was be­com­ing a Julius Caesar.

Power had been con­cen­trated in him, it said. He was sur­rounded by syco­phants and dis­missed peo­ple with a wave of his hand. Readers should get to­gether and de­throne him. It was signed Chanakya.

Some years later it turned out that the au­thor was Nehru him­self. “Can you imag­ine a sit­ting prime min­is­ter of India pub­lish­ing an ar­ti­cle say­ing that this Prime Minister has be­come too pow­er­ful and this is not a healthy state of af­fairs,” Shah said. {108-S08}
~ It is his favourite Nehru story. Generations from now, Shah said, peo­ple will scarcely be­lieve that such a per­son walked the earth.
stories.why: A sit­ting leader sound­ing the alarm about his own power is the op­po­site of a politician’s in­stinct. Shah also ad­mired Nehru’s ease with him­self: a happy man who joked about him­self and needed no strong­man pose. {108-C09}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Chanakya letter

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Manmohan Singh he met
stories.head: From the back row to the front
body: Between his spells in power, Manmohan Singh was a pri­vate cit­i­zen in Delhi. Ajay Shah, then a young re­searcher in Bombay in­vited to give talks, kept see­ing him slip into a back seat, lis­ten, and say al­most noth­ing.

In 2019 Vijay Kelkar asked Singh to re­lease the first edi­tion of *In Service of the Republic*, the book he wrote with Shah. Singh was un­well, and de­clined to be an­nounced as chief guest in case he could not come. {108-R24}
Then, with­out any an­nounce­ment, he came, sat in the front row, shook Shah’s hand and said: “This is a very im­por­tant book, thank you for writ­ing it.” {108-S14}
~ In those Delhi talks, Shah re­called, Singh spoke up only once, to dis­agree. “He never made it un­com­fort­able. He never threw his weight around.”
stories.why: Shah sees this quiet de­cency as Manmohan Singh’s method: decades spent learn­ing how India’s in­sti­tu­tions work, coali­tions built gen­tly and a cli­mate of opin­ion slowly moved. “That’s how a par­a­digm shifts,” he said.

quiz.a: Percy Mistry, by per­sonal cheque; the money was re­paid when fund­ing re­sumed.

quiz.q: What did Volodymyr Zelenskyy say when he was offered a way out of Kyiv?
quiz.a: “My place is here, I need am­mu­ni­tion, not a ride.”

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 108. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Václav Havel (Ondřej Sláma, CC BY-SA 3.0); Mark Carney (Bryan Berlin, CC BY-SA 4.0); Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Press Service of the President of Ukraine, CC BY 4.0); Mahatma Gandhi (Elliott & Fry, public domain); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Open Library and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Havel: A Life
shelf.creator: Michael Zantovsky
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great bi­og­ra­phy and finds a ‘stirring’ por­trait of Havel’s self-education in it.

shelf.title: The Garden Party and Other Plays
shelf.creator: Václav Havel
shelf.why: He says they are hi­lar­i­ous, avail­able in English and worth read­ing in full.

shelf.title: Letters to Olga
shelf.creator: Václav Havel
shelf.why: Amit calls it beau­ti­ful and quotes a line that sends a chill up his spine: ‘If I am to be pun­ished, let it be for who I am.

shelf.title: The Power of the Powerless
shelf.creator: Václav Havel
shelf.why: He calls it a won­der­ful ex­tended essay and notes the lat­est edi­tion has an in­tro­duc­tion by Timothy Snyder, also worth read­ing.

shelf.title: To the Castle and Back
shelf.creator: Václav Havel
shelf.why: Amit calls it a won­der­ful book.

shelf.title: Charter 77
shelf.creator: Václav Havel and co-signatories
shelf.why: It is the doc­u­ment be­hind Havel’s line to a hes­i­tant sig­na­tory: ‘you have al­ready taken a side, just not the one that you think you have.’

shelf.title: The Jackson Katz quote on passive sentence constructions
shelf.creator: Jackson Katz
shelf.why: It shows how the pas­sive voice (‘how many women were raped’ rather than ‘how many men raped women’) takes the focus off the men com­mit­ting vi­o­lence.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Amit’s most pop­u­lar Seen and the Unseen episode, a con­ver­sa­tion with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the ‘anti-uncle’ label) on the eco­nomic and so­cial lives of Indian women.

shelf.title: Salil Tripathi and the Gujaratis (Episode 409, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Salil Tripathi
shelf.why: Salil Tripathi tells the Havel and Mandela sto­ries that Amit uses to show how power changes peo­ple, in­clud­ing Havel’s moral clar­ity in power.

shelf.title: Arvind Kejriwal’s interview by Sudhir Chaudhary
shelf.creator: Sudhir Chaudhary
shelf.why: Amit calls it an in­ter­est­ing in­ter­view in which Kejriwal is called out on his hypocrisy.

shelf.title: Where Have All The Leaders Gone?
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s pub­lic-choice an­swer to why the free­dom strug­gle at­tracted peo­ple of prin­ci­ple while today’s cen­tralised state at­tracts ca­reerists chas­ing power and money.

shelf.title: The Vintage Book of Indian Writing 1947–1997
shelf.creator: Salman Rushdie and Elizabeth West (eds.)
shelf.why: An an­thol­ogy that opens with Nehru’s ‘Tryst with Destiny’, which Ajay calls one of the tran­scen­den­tal pieces of Indian writ­ing and ev­i­dence that great lead­ers can con­vey com­plex ideas.

shelf.title: Glimpses of World History
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: Nehru’s let­ters to his daugh­ter Indira, a his­tory of the world writ­ten from prison largely from mem­ory.

shelf.title: The Discovery of India
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: The book Ajay calls ‘lit­er­ally the book that in­vents the idea of India’: an idea grounded in his­tory and free of ha­tred, in a mod­ern syn­the­sis com­fort­able with sci­ence and lib­eral democ­racy.

shelf.title: A Tryst With Destiny
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: Ajay urges lis­ten­ers to step out of the cliché and read it with fresh eyes, as tran­scen­den­tal writ­ing.

shelf.title: The Light Has Gone Out of Our Lives
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: He says that raspy voice still does some­thing to you across all these years.

shelf.title: Letters to Chief Ministers
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: They show a prime min­is­ter who wrote co­pi­ously and clearly.

shelf.title: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
shelf.creator: Mahatma Gandhi
shelf.why: Ninety-nine vol­umes, free to read, in which you can watch a man en­gage with the world in writ­ing every day, with un­var­nished hon­esty, like a blog­ger of his time.

shelf.title: The Collected Writings and Speeches of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar
shelf.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
shelf.why: More than sixty vol­umes of Ambedkar’s writ­ings and speeches, free on­line and ‘amaz­ing to read’.

shelf.title: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay on what 1991 achieved and left un­done (fac­tor mar­kets, agri­cul­ture), and how free­ing parts of the econ­omy set off the dis­cov­ery and trade be­hind India’s growth spurt.

shelf.title: The 1991 Project
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s trea­sure trove of chron­i­cles and oral his­to­ries of the 1991 re­forms, in­clud­ing the leg­endary ‘M document’.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
shelf.why: Montek Singh Ahluwalia’s first-hand ac­count of his decades in the re­form en­gine room and the ‘silent revolution’ that built up from the late 1970s.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Servant of the People
shelf.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
shelf.why: The TV show in which Zelenskyy played Ukraine’s pres­i­dent be­fore be­com­ing it for real: the im­prob­a­ble start­ing point of the most un­likely ac­ci­den­tal-politician story.

shelf.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy playing the piano with his d***
shelf.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
shelf.why: A clip from Zelenskyy’s com­edy days that shows how im­prob­a­ble his jour­ney from co­me­dian to wartime leader was, and makes Amit’s point that mak­ing a fool of your­self on stage night after night takes courage too.

shelf.title: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with MR Madhavan on how India’s par­lia­men­tary rules, es­pe­cially the anti-defection law, weaken its democ­racy.

shelf.title: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit links Mao’s grand de­signs to de­mon­eti­sa­tion through one shared delu­sion, that a leader can re­design so­ci­ety to a mas­ter plan, and calls de­mon­eti­sa­tion the largest as­sault on prop­erty rights in human his­tory.

shelf.title: The Insider
shelf.creator: PV Narasimha Rao
shelf.why: Rao’s insider’s po­lit­i­cal skill made Manmohan Singh’s eco­nom­ics po­lit­i­cally pos­si­ble.

shelf.title: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
shelf.why: Vinay Sitapati on why Narasimha Rao de­serves much of the credit for the 1991 re­forms, and on the re­form­ers around him.

shelf.title: Don’t Run a Country Like a Company (Episode 60, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why busi­ness in­tu­itions don’t carry over to pub­lic pol­icy: pol­i­cy­mak­ing is a com­pletely dif­fer­ent and hard-won body of knowl­edge, and for­get­ting that is the trap be­hind many calls for in­dus­trial pol­icy.

shelf.title: Yes Minister
shelf.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
shelf.why: Among the loveli­est and fun­ni­est books Ajay has read, with real in­sight into pol­i­tics and the dif­fi­culty of change; its satire of re­flex­ive pol­i­cy­mak­ing (‘we must do some­thing, this is something’) ex­plains why price caps are the de­fault po­lit­i­cal re­sponse.

shelf.title: Yes Prime Minister
shelf.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
shelf.why: Ajay calls both of them mas­ter­pieces.

laughs.text: Amit asks whether Ajay would ac­cept ab­so­lute power, given that ‘power cor­rupts and ab­so­lute power cor­rupts ab­so­lutely.’ Ajay: ‘Power cor­rupts, but ab­so­lute power is pretty cool… get a bet­ter con­sti­tu­tion of India. What bet­ter use of ab­so­lute power?’
Ajay on Watergate as the scan­dal that led to Jimmy Carter: ‘Oh how help­less we were in those days, we thought that those are dread­ful things. Standards of crime have changed.’

Amit’s lim­er­ick on pol­i­tics, from his days as the Times of India’s weekly lim­er­ick writer (‘the world’s only paid lim­er­ick writer, I think’): ‘A neta who loves cur­rency notes / told me what his line of work de­notes. / It is kind of funny, we steal people’s money / and use some of it to buy their votes.’
Amit adapts Kipling and C.L.R. James: ‘What do they know of pol­i­tics who only pol­i­tics know?’
Ajay on Zelenskyy ral­ly­ing his peo­ple, cit­ing the line about Churchill that ‘he picked up the words of the English lan­guage and hurled them into bat­tle.’
